name: Chinchorro red body paint

lead: The Chinchorro of what is now northern Chile and southern Peru preserved their dead artificially, among the earliest known examples. In the "red mummy" style, dated roughly 2570-2090 BCE, the body was covered in red ochre while the face was usually left black.

The finish was part of a broader work of rebuilding the body: modelled faces, wigs of human hair and pigment coats. Archaeologists generally read it as part of an ancestor cult rather than a cosmetic in the modern sense.

paras: Embalmers dried the body cavities, packed them, placed wooden poles under the skin, sewed incisions, modelled the face and attached a wig fixed with black manganese paste, then coated the body in red ochre.
This is an archaeological subject with no modern practice. Red ochre is a mineral pigment; the entry is documented as history, not as a technique.

chain: Red ochre applied over the body
angle.text: The paint gave the preserved dead a finished, striking presentation within Chinchorro ritual. It is a historical example of colour used on the body to shape how a person is seen.

lead: Chinchorro red body paint refers to the red ochre coating applied to the artificially mummified bodies of the Chinchorro culture, a coastal fishing people of the Atacama region who lived from about 7000 to 1500 BCE between Ilo in Peru and Antofagasta in Chile.[1] Artificial mummification began around 5050 BCE and ended around 1800 BCE.[2]

The finish was part of a deliberately sculpted appearance: faces were modelled, human-hair wigs attached, and the surface coloured, first black with manganese and later red.[2] In 2021 the Chinchorro sites were inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List.[1]

paras: In the red style the body was not fully taken apart. Incisions at points such as the shoulders and groin allowed organs and some muscle to be removed, and the head was detached to remove the brain. Cavities were dried with hot coals and ashes and packed with materials such as seabird feathers, soil and camelid fibre; wooden poles supported the skin and the incisions were sewn shut.[2] The head was reattached with a long wig, sometimes about 60 cm, held with black manganese paste, the face was modelled, and the body was covered in red ochre, with the face generally left black.[2]

Earlier black mummies (about 5000-2800 BCE) were dismantled and rebuilt with sticks and clay, and coated in manganese-based black paint, leaving the wig unpainted.[2] The styles overlap in time and sometimes occur in the same cemetery.[2]

Researchers have proposed that mummification helped the soul survive or kept bodies from frightening the living, but the more widely accepted view is an ancestor cult, since bodies travelled with groups and were honoured in rituals before final burial.[2]
